ABCS: Small and mid-sized US companies bought directly and through other funds, spread across banks, health care, consumer brands and technology. It targets the cheaper, overlooked middle of the market where active managers hunt for value, so it complements a large-company core rather than replacing it.
AGIQ: Companies that earn a real share of their revenue from agentic AI, software that can plan and carry out tasks on its own, led by technology at over half. It is a narrow theme bet on the next wave of artificial intelligence, reaching beyond chipmakers into health care and industry.
AIHY: Companies building the giant data centers behind artificial intelligence: chipmakers, cloud platforms, networking and the firms that run AI models at huge scale. It is a concentrated growth bet on AI infrastructure spending, so it can swing sharply when enthusiasm for the AI buildout cools or heats up.
ALDB: Four deep buffer funds, each built to absorb a substantial slice of S&P 500 losses over its own outcome period, staggered so one resets every quarter. The ladder smooths out the timing risk of a single buffer start date, at the cost of capped gains in strong markets.
ARIA: A concentrated portfolio of just a few dozen companies from the US and other developed and emerging markets, with technology over half. With so few holdings it is a high-conviction bet on the manager's best ideas, so single stocks can move the whole fund noticeably.
AVIE: US companies in industries the managers expect to hold up when inflation climbs, with health care and energy the biggest groups at nearly three-tenths each. It is a defensive tilt for stock portfolios worried about rising prices, favoring businesses with pricing power over fast growers.
BESO: Direct holdings of the three most established cryptocurrencies: bitcoin, ether and Solana, some of them staked to earn extra rewards. It is a one-ticker way to own the core of the crypto market through a normal brokerage account, with all the sharp swings that come with digital coins.
BETH: Bitcoin and ether bought through futures contracts, split between the two in line with their market size, which leaves bitcoin the bigger share. It gives stock-market access to the two largest cryptocurrencies without a crypto account, though futures pricing can drift from the coins themselves and both swing wildly.
BFIX: Mostly short-term, high-quality bonds from US and foreign issuers, with a small options layer linked to stocks for extra kick. The bonds aim for steady income with modest rate risk, while the options can add gains in strong stock markets, an unusual mix for a bond fund.
BKLG: Large US companies selected for growth, meaning businesses expected to expand sales and profits faster than average, typically led by technology and consumer brands. It plays the growth role in a portfolio, favoring future potential over dividends or cheap prices, so it tends to swing more than the broad market.
BNDD: Long-term Treasury bonds, mostly held through a Treasury fund, combined with options tied to the shape of the interest rate curve. It is built as a hedge for deflation and slowing growth, the kind of scare that hits stocks hard, so it aims to gain when the economy weakens rather than when it grows.
CAS: Stocks listed on mainland China's own exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing, plus an options overlay that adds an income stream on top. It offers direct exposure to China's domestic market, which foreigners can otherwise reach only in limited ways, along with the currency and political risks that come with it.
CLUB: A hand-picked portfolio of global companies, weighted toward technology at about a third, with consumer brands, media and telecom making up much of the rest. It is an actively managed, concentrated stock picker's fund rather than a broad market holding, so its results hinge on the manager's choices, for better or worse.
COPA: Copper mining companies from around the world, from big producers to smaller explorers and refiners of the metal. Copper goes into wiring, power grids and electric vehicles, so the fund is a focused bet on industrial and clean-energy demand, and it swings with the copper price.
DLMY: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to gain from moves in either direction, rising when the market climbs and when it falls a little, over a one-year period ending in May. In exchange it gives up gains beyond a cap, so it is a cushion holding for investors who cannot call the market's direction.
EDGE: US large-company stocks, reached through index funds and options in a mix that mirrors the broad market, with technology about two-fifths. The options layer is there to sharpen returns beyond a plain index fund, which also magnifies swings, so it is a more aggressive take on a core stock holding.
EDGQ: The companies of the Nasdaq-100, held directly and through funds, combined with call options sold against them to generate weekly income. Selling the calls caps some of the upside of a tech-heavy index, trading part of its growth for a steadier stream of cash payouts.
EMES: A hand-picked set of emerging-market companies, concentrated in technology at about half, from chip and internet giants to banks and manufacturers. Active stock pickers run it as a best-ideas portfolio, so it can pull away from the broad emerging-market index in either direction.
EQLT: Stocks from emerging markets chosen for quality: strong profits, steady earnings and low debt compared with local rivals, led by technology at about a third. It aims to keep the growth potential of markets like China, Taiwan and India while skipping their shakiest companies.
FIZY: A concentrated portfolio of must-have growth stocks in the manager's view, led by technology at about two-fifths, with an options overlay on top. The overlay is meant to add income and soften drops, so the fund blends aggressive stock picking with a partial safety net.
HFEQ: A hedge-fund-style mix of long and short positions in stock funds and index futures, aiming to profit from both rising and falling names. It tries to deliver equity-like returns with less dependence on the market's direction, though the borrowed exposure means fees and swings run higher than a plain stock fund.
IBMW: Municipal bonds that mature around 2034, paying interest free of federal income tax and the alternative minimum tax. The fund is designed to wind up near the end of 2034 and hand the money back, making it a date-certain holding for a goal in that year.
ILIT: Companies around the world that mine lithium or turn it into battery materials, the metal at the heart of electric vehicle and storage batteries. It is a focused bet on the electric vehicle supply chain, so it rises and falls with lithium prices and battery demand rather than the wider market.
JANH: Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 that pay regular income as long as the market stays above the barrier level named in the fund's title. If the market ends a period below that barrier, losses follow the index down, so the cushion is real but not complete.
JDIV: Dividend-paying companies from around the world that have a record of growing or sustaining generous payouts, led by technology at about a third and banks and insurers next. It aims to deliver income plus growth from proven payers, so it suits a core stock role with a steadier, cash-returning tilt.
LJAN: Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 that pay an income stream while absorbing the first slice of market losses named in the fund's title. It is built for investors who want stock-market-linked income with a cushion, trading away most upside and renewing its terms each period, with this series starting in January.
MEMA: Actively managed stocks from emerging markets such as Asia and Latin America, led by technology at nearly two-fifths and banks next. The managers pick winners and can trim exposure when they see trouble, aiming for emerging-market growth with some protection, though these markets still swing hard.
MFIG: Fast-growing, innovative companies chosen by a Motley Fool index, led by technology at about half, with media, health care and consumer brands behind. It is a growth-tilted stock holding that favors disruptors over steady earners, so expect bigger swings than the broad market.
MSFY: Options that mimic owning Microsoft stock, backed by Treasury bills and other bonds held as collateral. It sells options to pay regular income, which caps the gains when Microsoft climbs, so it is an income-first way to follow one giant software stock.
MUYY: An income strategy built on options tied to a leveraged fund on Micron, the memory chip maker, rather than on the stock itself. It sells options to harvest the extra premium that a fast-moving leveraged fund generates, aiming for large payouts while taking amplified downside when the chip stock falls.
MYCL: Corporate bonds from US companies that mostly come due in 2032, held as a date-targeted income portfolio. It suits money aimed at a goal around 2032: interest payments along the way, company credit risk throughout, and rate risk that fades as the due dates approach.
MYMJ: Municipal bonds from US states and cities that mostly come due in 2030, paying interest that is exempt from federal income tax. It suits savers aiming at a goal around 2030, with tax-free income along the way and risk that eases as the bonds near their due dates.
NVIT: Options that create synthetic exposure to one stock, chipmaker Nvidia, with Treasury bills as collateral. Its stated goal is cash payouts adding up to about a quarter of the fund's value each year, funded by option premiums, which makes it an aggressive income play on a single fast-moving stock.
OILT: Oil and gas producers whose wells are in Texas, from the big shale drillers to smaller independents, weighted by the value of what they produce. It is a narrow bet on the Texas energy patch, so it lives and dies with oil prices and drilling activity in one state.
PWER: Companies across the whole energy transition: oil and gas firms, utilities, miners of battery and grid metals, and industrial suppliers. It spreads the shift to cleaner energy across four industries instead of betting on one, so it moves with energy prices as much as with green spending.
PYPY: Options built around a single stock, PayPal, paired with Treasury bills held as collateral. It sells call options to turn PayPal's price moves into regular cash payouts, which caps how much it gains when the stock jumps, so it is an income play on one company rather than a way to own it.
QQHG: The big non-bank companies of the Nasdaq, mostly technology at about three-fifths, paired with an options overlay that cushions part of any fall. It keeps the growth engine of the Nasdaq-100 while softening its drops, in exchange for giving up some return in strong rallies.
QSML: Small US companies screened for both quality and growth, meaning profitable firms that are still expanding, led by technology at about a quarter. It aims for the faster-growing corner of the small-cap market without the shakiest balance sheets, a satellite growth holding rather than a core one.
RANK: Fifty US stocks chosen by combining analyst ratings with price momentum, leaning heavily to technology at over two-fifths. It is a rules-based momentum bet that chases what is already working, so it can shine in strong markets and snap back hard when trends reverse.
REK: A trading tool that bets against US real estate stocks, aiming to move opposite to property companies in the S&P 500 each day. Because the bet resets daily, results drift away from a simple mirror image over longer stretches, so it is built for short holding periods, not long-term investing.
RFCI: Bonds from companies and governments around the world, across all maturities and credit ratings, plus a small slice of preferred stock. The managers move money between bond types as conditions change, aiming for steady income with flexibility, so it fits the core bond role while taking more credit risk than a plain index fund.
SHRT: US stocks held both long and short, with the short side bigger, leaving the fund about half net short overall. It is a bearish hedge built by stock pickers who bet against companies they see as overpriced, so it tends to gain when the stock market falls and lose when it rises.
SMLL: Small US companies, roughly the size range of the Russell 2000, picked actively with industrials and regional banks the biggest groups. Small stocks offer more growth potential than big ones but swing harder, and the active approach means the fund leans on the managers' stock picking rather than holding the whole small-cap market.
SPDG: Dividend-paying companies drawn from a broad US stock index, arranged so each industry's weight matches the wider market instead of piling into the usual high-yield corners. The result is income from stocks without the heavy lean toward utilities and staples that most dividend funds have, keeping it closer to a core holding.
SUPP: Companies rebuilding and reshoring supply chains: manufacturers, logistics and factory technology firms, with industrials near half and technology close behind. It is a bet on production moving closer to home and getting more automated, picked actively rather than spread across the whole market.
TDOT: Direct ownership of DOT, the token of the Polkadot network, with the holdings staked to validators to earn extra tokens as rewards. It wraps a single cryptocurrency in a stock-market fund, so the price swings are large and the staking yield, not any business earnings, is the only return on top.
WABF: A core-plus bond portfolio of US and foreign debt across maturities, mostly high quality, with room for up to a fifth in lower-rated bonds for extra yield. Active managers adjust the mix as rates and credit conditions change, aiming for steady income with a bit more reach than a plain core fund.
WCEO: US companies of all sizes that share one trait: each is run by a woman chief executive, spread across banking, technology, retail and industry. It is a values-based way to own a broad slice of the stock market, with the screen based on who leads the company rather than what it sells.
WMTI: Options that give magnified exposure to a single stock, retail giant Walmart, alongside an income stream from selling options. It pairs leveraged growth on one company with regular payouts, so it moves harder than the stock itself and is a concentrated trading-style holding, not a diversified one.
XRPM: Options sold on funds that hold XRP, the Ripple-linked cryptocurrency, aiming to collect about 3% of the fund's value in option premium each month, as its name states. It also keeps some exposure to XRP's price, so payouts ride on one volatile coin and can shrink when markets go quiet.
